topic: chasing a clean copper red glaze through reduction firing in a small gas kiln

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: pirometr z zapisem

base: I fire a small gas kiln and I am trying to get a clean copper red on stoneware.
An older kiln stands in the same shed, electric and rather tired, which I use for bisque.
A logging pyrometer sits on the bench and records the whole climb for me afterwards.
The copper glaze keeps coming out a dull liver colour rather than the bright red I want.
Should I start reduction earlier in the firing, or change the glaze recipe instead?
Change the firing before you touch the recipe, because copper reds live and die on atmosphere.
Begin reduction around nine hundred degrees, well before the glaze has sealed over the body.
If you wait until the surface melts, the copper cannot reduce and stays a muddy brown.
Hold a steady, gentle reduction rather than a heavy one, since soot buys you nothing here.
I began reduction at nine hundred and held the damper steady for most of the climb.
The red is far better now, though patches near the door came out grey and lifeless.
The logging pyrometer shows that the door side ran forty degrees cooler for two whole hours.
The older kiln never showed such a difference, but it was electric and much smaller.
Is that temperature gap enough to explain the grey patches, or is something else at fault?
Forty degrees is more than enough, because copper reds sit in a very narrow window.
Cooler ware also sees a different atmosphere, since flame moves fastest where the kiln is hottest.
Try shifting the shelves outward by a finger's width to let flame reach the door side.
Then fire once more without altering anything else, so you know what the change actually did.
I moved the shelves out and the door side came within fifteen degrees of the rest.
Most of the pots are now a good deep red, with only slight mottling near the base.
The mottling looks almost like the glaze has crawled a little away from the foot ring.
Could that be a fault in the application, or is it still something to do with firing?
Crawling near a foot ring is nearly always application, not firing, in my long experience.
Dust or wax resist on the pot keeps the glaze from wetting the clay properly.
Wipe each foot with a damp sponge before dipping, and let the pot dry fully.
Thick application over a dusty surface will crawl however carefully you manage the atmosphere.
I sponged every foot before dipping and the crawling has gone from the whole batch.
One tall bottle still shows a run down one side where the glaze pooled heavily.
It stuck slightly to the shelf, though a chisel took it off without much damage.
Should I thin the glaze for tall pieces, or simply dip them for a shorter count?
Dip for a shorter count, because thinning the whole bucket will spoil your flatter work.
Tall forms hold more glaze on the lower half whatever consistency you happen to mix.
Count two seconds instead of four and lift the bottle out with a smooth motion.
Wax the foot and a finger's width above it, so any run stops before the shelf.
The shorter dip worked and the last firing came out without a single stuck pot.
I now have a firing that I would happily repeat, which feels strange after so long.
The whole cycle takes eleven hours and the cooling seems to matter as much as the climb.
Is there any sense in slowing the cooling further, or have I reached the useful limit?
Slow cooling helps copper reds, but only through the first two hundred degrees below peak.
Below that the colour is fixed and further patience buys you nothing except fuel bills.
Damper down tightly at the end and let the kiln fall on its own overnight.
Write the whole schedule down now, because a repeatable firing is worth more than any recipe.
